claims.text: Applying a thin, surface-deposited Al2O3-rich coating to a refractory high-entropy alloy will significantly improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance.
The Al2O3-rich coating forms a continuous barrier on the alloy surface.
The alumina barrier limits oxygen diffusion into the underlying alloy.
As-cast or conventionally processed refractory high-entropy alloys typically form non-protective oxide scales under high-temperature oxidative conditions.
Chemical vapor deposition or physical vapor deposition can be used to apply the proposed thin, dense Al2O3-rich coating.
The coating should provide protection during exposure to air at approximately 1100 degrees Celsius for up to 100 hours.
The preformed continuous alumina scale acts as an oxygen-diffusion barrier.
The Al2O3 coating remains stable at high temperature.
The Al2O3 coating remains adherent at high temperature.
The Al2O3 protective layer grows slowly at high temperature.
Delaying oxygen ingress reduces formation of deleterious oxide phases in the underlying refractory high-entropy alloy.
The deleterious oxide phases can compromise the alloy's mechanical integrity.
At 1100 degrees Celsius in air, the coated alloy will have at least 50% less oxidation weight gain than an untreated control.
Untreated specimens exposed to air at 1100 degrees Celsius develop thicker and less protective oxide scales than coated specimens.
Untreated specimens exposed to air at 1100 degrees Celsius exhibit greater oxidation weight gain than coated specimens.
The coating's protective performance may vary with substantially longer exposure or oxygen partial pressures different from atmospheric levels.
Coating adhesion and integrity under thermal cycling are uncertain.
The magnitude of improvement may depend on coating-process details and alloy-specific interactions.
